title: Meal prep for busy executives: how to plan the cooking week
body_markdown:
Executive household meal prep is planned cooking around a demanding diary, with the aim of keeping household meals ready when you need them. An executive household meal prep brief should tell the cook who is eating, which meals need covering, what changes during travel weeks and how the kitchen works—not simply list favourite dishes.


**TL;DR**

- An executive household meal prep brief starts with attendance, meal coverage and dietary requirements—not a recipe list.
- myCHEF suits households seeking vetted chefs for home-cooked meals and weekly meal prep.
- Separate office lunches, family dinners and travel-day meals so each has clear portions and handling instructions.
- Agree shopping, containers, kitchen access and changes before confirming the cooking schedule.


If you are still choosing between cooking at home and receiving prepared meals, start with the [meal prep services guide](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/best-meal-prep-services-in-dubai). Use that comparison to choose a service format; use this guide to write the working brief for your household.

## Why meal prep matters for executive households

A busy household does not necessarily need more food. It needs the right meals available at the right moments. A lunch packed for the office, a dinner eaten after a late meeting and a family meal served while you are travelling each need different instructions.

**Plan around attendance before planning around recipes.** Otherwise, even a carefully chosen menu leaves practical questions unanswered: who receives each portion, who reheats it and what happens when the diary changes?

Separate recurring household cooking from entertaining. A birthday dinner or an evening with guests needs its own service brief, even if the guest count is small. Adding it to the weekly meal plan without discussing service, staffing and timing creates an unclear scope.

The brief also gives everyone a shared reference. Your chef, household contact and anyone serving the food should work from the same menu, portion plan and instructions rather than separate messages.

## How to write the household cooking brief

### Map the meals you actually need

Start with your calendar and a simple shared document. Mark meals at home, meals away, travel days and occasions when other household members need food without you. This manual version is enough to reveal the cooking requirement before you discuss a service.

Do not count every weekday as a full cooking day by default. Distinguish meals you want prepared from meals you will buy elsewhere, eat at a meeting or cook yourself. That prevents a broad request for healthy meals from becoming an unnecessarily large menu.

For an illustrative household of 2 adults, covering 3 office lunches each means 6 lunch portions. Family dinners are a separate count. This is planning arithmetic, not a recommended package or a standard service quantity.

- Mark attendance against each meal, not just each date.
- Separate packed lunches from meals eaten at home.
- Identify meals needed while you are travelling.
- Flag late arrivals and different dinner times.
- Name one person responsible for confirming diary changes.

### Define portions and dietary requirements

Write a short profile for each person before choosing dishes. Include preferences, disliked ingredients, allergies and any instructions supplied by a qualified healthcare professional. Keep preferences and safety requirements clearly separate.

Avoid vague labels such as clean eating or high protein without explaining what you mean. Describe the food you enjoy, the meals you need and any professionally advised requirements. Do not ask a chef to infer a medical diet from a general goal.

If you want help turning those details into household cooking, myCHEF provides vetted chefs for home-cooked meals and weekly meal prep. Suitability still depends on the brief: confirm that the proposed menu and preparation arrangements address your stated requirements before agreeing the service.

**Record requirements per person, not as one household average.** A shared main dish can still need different accompaniments or portion sizes; ask how those differences will be handled.

- List allergies separately from preferences and dislikes.
- Record requirements against each person's name.
- Describe portion preferences using familiar meal examples.
- Identify meals that need individual packaging.
- Request written confirmation of dietary arrangements.

### Choose dishes by how they will be eaten

Build the menu around the eating occasion. A dish served immediately from the kitchen is not the same task as a packed lunch carried to work or a dinner reheated later. Tell the cook where the food will be eaten and what equipment is available there.

Begin with meals you already enjoy. Then discuss which components should be prepared ahead, kept separate or finished close to serving. This gives the cook a practical starting point without requiring you to design a professional menu.

An illustrative menu might pair a grain bowl with separately packed dressing for lunch, a stew with an accompanying side for dinner, and prepared vegetables for a meal finished at home. These are examples to discuss, not a myCHEF menu or confirmed package.

Ask for dish-specific handling and reheating instructions. Do not assume that everything prepared during one visit should remain refrigerated until the end of the week; agree what is intended for earlier meals, later preparation or freezing.

- Assign each dish to a named meal slot.
- State whether it will be eaten hot or cold.
- Describe the reheating equipment at home and work.
- Identify components that should stay separate.
- Request storage and reheating instructions for each dish.

### Agree shopping and kitchen responsibilities

Check the kitchen yourself before the first cooking visit. Note available equipment, usable preparation space, refrigerator and freezer capacity, and the containers you already own. Describe what is actually available rather than assuming a household kitchen is fully equipped.

Then divide responsibilities explicitly. Shopping, ingredient approval, substitutions, container provision and cleaning are separate tasks. Ask which are included in the proposal and which remain with you; do not treat an unstated task as an agreed inclusion.

Dubai households should also explain building access and practical arrival arrangements. Tell the cook about reception procedures, parking instructions and the route to the kitchen. These details belong in the brief, not in a last-minute exchange when someone is already outside.

**Agree the handover as carefully as the cooking.** Decide where prepared food goes, how portions are labelled and who receives the final instructions.

- Record essential equipment and any missing items.
- Confirm who buys ingredients and approves substitutions.
- Agree who supplies containers and labels.
- Explain access, parking and kitchen entry arrangements.
- Confirm cleaning responsibilities and food handover.

### Set a cooking rhythm and a change process

Start by placing your required meals on the calendar. Then discuss a cooking schedule that fits the menu, the household's access arrangements and the intended storage plan. Do not choose a visit pattern solely because it sounds convenient.

Give travel weeks their own version of the brief. If you are away but your family remains at home, the cooking requirement changes rather than disappears. If everyone is away, communicate that clearly instead of leaving the regular plan unchanged.

For example, an illustrative diary might cover 4 evenings at home and 2 office-lunch days. A changed meeting schedule should trigger an attendance update, not an automatic addition of more dishes. Ask how menu changes, cancellations and extra requests are handled before confirming the arrangement.

Keep one current document. A shared calendar identifies attendance; the meal brief records what the cook should prepare. Neither should depend on someone finding the latest instruction in a long message thread.

- Confirm cooking dates and access windows.
- Create a separate version for travel weeks.
- Agree how and when to communicate changes.
- Record the process for additional meal requests.
- Keep the approved menu in one shared location.

### Review the handover before repeating the plan

After the first cooking cycle, compare the brief with what your household actually used. Record meals eaten, portions left over, dishes enjoyed and any confusing instructions. A simple note is more useful than a broad judgement that the service was good or disappointing.

Review food and process separately. You might enjoy the menu but need smaller portions, clearer labels or a different cooking time. Specific feedback makes those decisions easier to discuss without replacing the entire plan.

For myCHEF weekly meal prep, use the same household brief to explain what you want retained and what needs changing. Do not assume shopping, nutrition tracking or additional household duties are included; confirm each responsibility in the proposed scope.

Repeat what works. Change the attendance plan when your diary changes, and change dishes when your household feedback supports it.

- Record which meals were eaten and which remained.
- Note portion feedback for each household member.
- Identify unclear labels or reheating instructions.
- Separate menu changes from scheduling changes.
- Approve the next plan before shopping begins.

## What belongs in the final brief?

Keep the working document short enough to read before cooking. Use five headings: attendance, food requirements, meal plan, kitchen arrangements and responsibilities. Detailed dietary information can sit alongside it, but the main brief should make the day's work clear.


![Household brief organised around attendance, food requirements, meal planning, kitchen arrangements and responsibilities.](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/813e838e-ac1a-4cf1-9ed2-affdc12a1b1c/body-0ae8a7af5e4cc4d9e5748dc89260acb0.jpg)

*Agree the practical brief before expanding the menu.*


A useful brief distinguishes a requirement from a request. An allergy is a requirement; a preferred cuisine is a request. A confirmed kitchen access window is an arrangement; an extra dinner is a scope change. That distinction helps you ask precise questions when comparing proposals.

Include the date of the latest revision and the name of the household contact. Remove superseded instructions rather than leaving contradictory versions in the same document.

## Which cooking option fits your household?

Choose the format according to who will do the work and where cooking happens. None removes the need to explain dietary requirements, meal coverage and practical arrangements.

| Option | Best for | Practical advantage | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Household batch cooking | People who want direct control and can allocate kitchen time | You choose ingredients, dishes and portions yourself | Shopping, preparation and clearing remain your responsibility |
| Prepared meal delivery | Households seeking meals without cooking visits | Cooking takes place outside your home | Check how the offered menu, portions and dietary arrangements match your brief |
| Chef-led household meal prep | Households wanting cooking organised around their kitchen and family | You can discuss the menu alongside household routines | Kitchen access, responsibilities and the cooking schedule need agreement |
| A mixed arrangement | Households combining home cooking with meals sourced elsewhere | Different meal slots can use different formats | Someone must coordinate quantities and prevent overlap |

myCHEF is suited to households seeking vetted chefs for home-cooked meals and weekly meal prep. The service requires a clear household brief; it does not replace decisions about attendance, requirements or kitchen access.

When comparing proposals, separate ingredients, shopping, preparation, packaging, cleaning and any service at the table. Ask what is included, what is excluded and what changes the quote. Meal coverage, menu requirements, cooking frequency and agreed duties are useful points to discuss rather than assumptions to make.

## Common mistakes executive households make

### Planning for an ideal diary

A menu built around being home every evening does not match a week of travel and late meetings. **Brief for expected attendance, then agree a change process.** Give the cook updated information instead of asking them to guess which meals are still needed.

### Combining personal and family meals without a portion plan

Your office lunch and the family's dinner are different requirements. Count them separately, identify the recipients and explain how each will be served. A household total alone does not tell the cook how to package or divide the food.

### Delegating decisions without naming a contact

An executive assistant, household manager and family member can each provide useful information. Conflicting instructions still need resolving. Name one person to approve the menu and scope, with another contact available for access on the cooking day.

### Adding entertaining to the recurring brief

Guests change more than quantities. Serving style, timing, staffing and clearing need discussion. Treat a private dinner or celebration as a separate request rather than assuming the household cooking arrangement covers it.

## FAQ


**What should an executive household meal prep brief include?**

Include attendance, meal coverage, portions, dietary requirements, kitchen arrangements and responsibilities. Name the person who approves the menu and communicates changes.

**Is a private chef or prepared meal delivery better for a busy executive?**

Chef-led household cooking fits a brief centred on your kitchen and family routines; prepared meal delivery fits meals cooked elsewhere. Compare dietary arrangements, portion choices and the tasks that remain your responsibility.

**Can I plan different meals for myself and my family?**

Yes, you can specify separate meal requirements in the brief. Ask the provider how different dishes, portions and packaging affect the proposed scope.

**How many cooking visits should I request each week?**

Request a schedule based on meal coverage, the proposed dishes and the agreed storage plan. Confirm the pattern after discussing kitchen access and when each meal will be eaten.

**What happens to the meal plan when I travel?**

Update attendance and identify which household members still need meals. Agree the provider's process for changes before confirming the recurring arrangement.

**Does household meal prep include grocery shopping and cleaning?**

Shopping and cleaning must be confirmed in the proposal rather than assumed. Ask who buys ingredients, approves substitutions, provides containers and clears the kitchen.

**How should I communicate allergies or a medical diet?**

Record allergies clearly and provide any relevant instructions from your qualified healthcare professional. Ask the provider to confirm the proposed preparation arrangements before you agree the service.


## Related guides

- [Private chefs for home dining](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/best-private-chefs-in-dubai-for-home-dining) — a related starting point when your requirement is a meal served at home rather than prepared portions.

## Start with your next working week

The most useful first document is your attendance plan, not an elaborate menu. Once you know which meals need covering, you can discuss food, responsibilities and a cooking rhythm without guessing.

To enquire about myCHEF household meal prep, share your preferred start date, Dubai location, household diner count and service required. Include the meals you need covered, dietary requirements and travel pattern so the enquiry describes your actual cooking week.
